```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

library(tidyverse)
library(caret)
library(DataExplorer)
library(e1071)
library(corrplot)
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(randomForest)
library(pROC)
library(knitr)
```

### Import

```{r}
#df <- read.csv("breast-cancer.csv")
df_raw <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Chung-Brandon/621-Data-Mining/refs/heads/main/breast-cancer.csv")
```

### Clean & Tidy

```{r}
# Convert y variable to factor
df <- df_raw |> mutate(diagnosis = as.factor(diagnosis))

# Keep only the mean value columns
df <- df |>
  select(
    -id,
    -ends_with("_se"),          # drop all *_se columns
    -ends_with("_worst")        # drop all *_worst columns
  )
```

### Data Exploration

```{r}
# Check missing values
colSums(is.na(df))
```

```{r}
# Distribution of target variable
ggplot(df, aes(x = diagnosis)) +
  geom_bar()
```

```{r}
# Distribution of all other variables
plot_histogram(df)
```

### Correlation matrix

```{r}
# Convert factor names to binary: Malignant = 1, Benign = 0
df$diagnosis <- ifelse(df$diagnosis == "M", 1, 0)

corr_matrix <- cor(df, use = "complete.obs")
corrplot(corr_matrix, method = "color", type = "upper")
```

### Data Transformations

```{r}
# Log transform for skewed variables
numeric_cols <- sapply(df, is.numeric)
numeric_cols["diagnosis"] <- FALSE

skews <- apply(df[, numeric_cols], 2, skewness)
skews <- skews[-1] |> sort(decreasing = TRUE)

# Use log(x+1) of any variable with skew > 1
skews_log <- names(skews[skews > 1])
df_log <- df
df_log[, skews_log] <- log1p(df[, skews_log])

names(df_log)[names(df_log) %in% skews_log] <- paste0(skews_log, "_log")
names(df_log)
```

```{r}
# Standardize large variations with Z-score scaling (mean = 0, SD = 1)
df_log[, numeric_cols] <- scale(df_log[, numeric_cols])
```

```{r}
# Partition for training and testing
set.seed(123)

train_index <- createDataPartition(df_log$diagnosis, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)

train <- df_log[train_index, ]
test <- df_log[-train_index, ]
```

# Models

### Logistic Regression

```{r}
m1 <- glm(diagnosis ~ ., data = train, family = binomial)
summary(m1)
```

This preliminary logistic regression model is an improvement over the null, as per the reduction in deviance from 515.85 to 108.49. Of all the predictor variables, `texture_mean` is the most significant (p < 0.001), suggesting that higher texture values are strongly associated with increased odds of malignancy.

`smoothness_mean` and `compactness_mean_log` show borderline significance. The remaining variables are not relevant, so the 2nd model below drops them.

```{r}
m2 <- glm(diagnosis ~ texture_mean + smoothness_mean + compactness_mean_log, data = train, family = binomial)
summary(m2)
```

In this simplified model, both `texture_mean` (p < 0.001) and `compactness_mean_log` (p < 0.001) are highly significant, while `smoothness_mean` is not (p = 0.132), suggesting its effect is weak after accounting for the other two predictors.


Model #3
Decision Tree- chosen as it easy to interpret and easy to communicate with clinicans, captures non linear relationships (in the real world many biological variables interact in non linear ways.), handles well mixeed types of predictors, and fast to train and test.
```{r}
m3<-rpart(diagnosis~., data = train, method = "class")

#decision tree plot
rpart.plot(m3, main="Breast Cancer Classification Decision Tree Model")
```


Model #4 
Random Forest- is well-suited for this breast cancer classification task because it handles nonlinear interactions among tumor characteristics without requiring explicit specification. Robust to multicollinearity, which is important given the high correlation among many tumor measurements. Provides variable importance measures, offering insight into which features contribute most to classification. Performs well with high-dimensional data and minimal tuning. Typically yields strong predictive accuracy.
```{r}
set.seed(123)
m4<-randomForest(as.factor(diagnosis)~.,data = train, ntree=500, mtry=floor(sqrt(ncol(train)-1)),importance=TRUE)

print(m4)
```

## Model selection 

```{r}
# create eval function
eval_model <- function(true, prob, threshold = 0.5) {
  pred <- ifelse(prob > threshold, 1, 0)
  
  cm <- confusionMatrix(
    factor(pred),
    factor(true),
    positive = "1"
  )
  
  data.frame(
    Accuracy = cm$overall["Accuracy"],
    Sensitivity = cm$byClass["Sensitivity"],
    Specificity = cm$byClass["Specificity"],
    AUC = auc(roc(true, prob))
  )
}
```


```{r}
log_prob1<-predict(m1, test, type= "response")
log_results1<-eval_model(test$diagnosis, log_prob1)

log_prob2<-predict(m2, test, type= "response")
log_results2<-eval_model(test$diagnosis, log_prob2)

tree_prob<-predict(m3, test, type= "prob")[,2]
tree_results<-eval_model(test$diagnosis, tree_prob)

rf_prob<-predict(m4, test, type= "prob")[,2]
rf_results<-eval_model(test$diagnosis, rf_prob)
```


```{r}
results_table <- rbind(
  Logistic_Regression = log_results1,
  Logistic_Regression_Reduced = log_results2,
  Decision_Tree = tree_results,
  Random_Forest = rf_results
)

results_table <- round(results_table, 3)

kable(
  results_table,
  caption = "Model Performance Comparison")
```
